title: Criminal breach of trust vs cheating - key differences lawyers must know
p1: Two cases can involve the same money, the same transaction, and the same complaint — yet one may be cheating while the other is criminal breach of trust. The difference often turns on what happened at the beginning.
p2: The common misconception is that both offences simply mean “someone took another person’s money.” They do not. In cheating, dishonest intention is generally present when the person induces the other party to part with property. In criminal breach of trust, the property was entrusted or placed under someone’s control first, and the dishonest misuse or conversion happens afterward.
p3: That timing can be decisive. If A never intended to perform the promise and dishonestly induced B to pay, the facts may point toward cheating. If A legitimately received B’s property for a particular purpose but later dishonestly converted or used it contrary to that trust, breach of trust may be the stronger characterization. A failed promise, by itself, is not automatically cheating.
conclusion: For lawyers assessing a complaint, which fact would you examine first: the accused’s intention at the time of the transaction, or the circumstances surrounding the entrustment?
